opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a pretty big gap between what people assume these models can do and what they can actually do today, and that gap goes both ways. A lot of people still picture AI as a chatbot that answers trivia questions or writes a cute poem. They haven't seen what happens when you give a model a real task, the kind of thing a lawyer, an engineer, or a financial analyst would spend hours on, and it comes back with something genuinely useful.

Other people overestimate things. They see a flashy demo and assume the model can take over an entire job end to end, when in reality there are still real weaknesses: long-horizon tasks, getting the formatting exactly right, knowing when to ask for clarification, catching its own mistakes.

Part of the problem is that the way we've historically measured AI doesn't map onto how people think about work. We've had benchmarks like multiple-choice exams or competition math problems. Those are useful signals, but if you're a nurse or a paralegal, a score on a math olympiad doesn't tell you whether the model can help with your actual day. So a big motivation for the evaluation work I do is to measure model performance on tasks that look like real economically valuable work, built and graded by people who actually do those jobs. Then we can say concretely: on this kind of deliverable, experts prefer the model's output this often, and here's where it still falls short.

That gives everyone, from researchers to policymakers to someone deciding whether to use these tools at work, a much more grounded picture than either the hype or the skepticism.

r001.rationale: The response says some people underestimate what models can do now, but it does not say they underestimate how quickly models will become capable across many jobs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts useful performance on a real task with the ability to take over an entire job end to end.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how accurately people in software or research understand AI capabilities with people in other industries.

r004.rationale: The response mentions people not having seen models handle real tasks, but does not clearly identify firsthand use as a way for people to better understand model capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's actually a pretty big gap between how people talk about it and what's really going on. A lot of the public conversation is anchored on either demos or benchmarks, and both of those can be misleading in different directions.

On one side, you see a model do something impressive in a demo, like write a whole app or solve a hard math problem, and it's easy to extrapolate from that and assume it can do most of what a professional does. On the other side, people interact with a model, it makes a silly mistake, and they conclude it's basically a toy. Neither of those is a great picture of actual capability.

What we've found is that the honest answer is really task-dependent. Models are already quite strong on well-specified, self-contained tasks, especially ones where there's a lot of relevant text on the internet. But most real work isn't like that. It's long-horizon, it's ambiguous, you have to gather context, ask clarifying questions, and recover when something goes wrong halfway through. That's where models still struggle, and it's also where most of the economic value lives.

So part of why I care so much about evals is that they're how we try to close that gap in understanding. If you measure performance on tasks that actually look like the work people do, with real deliverables graded by domain experts, you get a much more grounded view. And a lot of the time, the result is that models are better than skeptics expect on some things, and worse than enthusiasts expect on others. The interesting part is figuring out exactly where that line is and how fast it's moving.

r001.rationale: The response describes a gap between public impressions and current capabilities, but does not say people underestimate how quickly models will become capable across many jobs.

r002.rationale: It contrasts models’ strength on well-specified, self-contained tasks with their difficulty handling long-horizon, ambiguous real work.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between how accurately software and research workers understand AI capabilities and people in other industries.

r004.rationale: It mentions people interacting with models, but does not identify firsthand use as a way to better understand their capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think people’s understanding is really shaped by what they’ve tried personally. If you’ve mostly used a model to answer questions or help write an email, you might think of it as a useful assistant for small tasks. You may not have a sense of how much of a longer workflow it can take on.

But there’s also a distinction between seeing a model do something impressive once and being able to rely on it to do that work consistently. Can it handle the messy context? Can it recognize when it’s missing information? How much checking does a person need to do afterward?

So I think we need to get more concrete about what we mean by “doing work.” Which task, under what conditions, and with how much human involvement? That’s a much more useful conversation than whether a model is broadly capable or not.

r002.rationale: It contrasts small tasks with longer workflows, but does not clearly distinguish individual tasks from carrying out entire jobs.

r003.rationale: It does not compare how accurately people in software and research understand model capabilities with people in other industries.

r004.rationale: It says people’s understanding is shaped by what they have personally tried, and explains that limited firsthand use may leave them unaware of models’ broader capabilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think people’s understanding is still catching up to what the models can actually do. A lot of people encounter AI by asking it a question and getting an answer, so they think of it as a chatbot. But doing work means something more: understanding a goal, taking several steps, using tools, and checking whether the result is right.

At the same time, being impressive on one task doesn’t mean a model can reliably take over an entire job. Most jobs are bundles of tasks, with context and judgment woven through them. So I think we need to get more specific: What can the model do independently? Where does it need human guidance? And how much effort does it take to verify the output? That’s a much more useful way to understand its capabilities than asking whether it’s generally smart.
